passage: Tuesday, 4:30. Today I was deep in the payroll mismatch, finally seeing the pattern in the numbers, when Chaitanya pinged: “Quick question, where's the template?” I answered in one line. The pattern was already fuzzy. Ten minutes later: “Sorry, one more, which version?” Then another, a small thing, then a fourth. Each one took me about two minutes, but each time I had to rebuild the whole picture from scratch. By six I'd found nothing new and my shoulders ached. I'm not angry at Chaitanya; the questions are reasonable. But I'm tired in a way that doesn't match the day. Tomorrow I'll put a note on my screen: “deep work, back at 11.” — Manoj

qa.q: What was Manoj working on when the first ping arrived?
qa.a: Manoj was working on the payroll mismatch when Chaitanya asked for the template.

qa.q: What is Manoj feeling by six o'clock?
qa.a: Manoj feels tired and frustrated, though not angry at Chaitanya, since each short question broke the thread.

qa.q: What does Manoj plan to do the next day?
qa.a: Manoj plans to put a note on the screen saying “deep work, back at 11” so the focus time is visible.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya see the four questions?
qa.a: Chaitanya probably sees them as small and harmless, and does not realise each two-minute answer costs Manoj much longer to recover.

grounding: A worker deep in a problem is repeatedly pinged and loses the thread each time.

passage: Devika, twenty-four, was the only engineer at the small water-board office in Karad. That Tuesday she had to finish the pipeline pressure calculations before the district officer's visit. Every ten minutes her colleague Hafsa came to her desk. "Just two minutes, which form for the pump repair?" Then, "Where's the stapler?" Then, "Can you check this letter?" Each question took a moment. But each time Devika returned to her sheet, she had to find the right row and remember her last number. By lunch she had done a quarter of the work. She finally said, "Hafsa, I'll be free at three. Can you keep a list till then?" Hafsa, a little surprised, agreed.

qa.q: Before whose visit did Devika need to finish the calculations?
qa.a: Before the district officer's visit.

qa.q: How did Devika feel by lunch?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and pressured, having done only a quarter of the work because of the repeated interruptions.

qa.q: What did Devika ask for, and why could it help?
qa.a: She asked Hafsa to keep a list until three, which lets her keep her focus and still answer every question later.

qa.q: How might Hafsa see those questions?
qa.a: Hafsa likely saw each question as small and quick, and was a little surprised to learn it was costing Devika so much.

grounding: Shows a worker repeatedly interrupted with quick questions and losing her place, then asking for questions to be batched.

passage: Santiago was debugging a payment error at a software company in Lima, the kind of problem where he had to hold six things in his head at once. Amara, from customer support, sent him a message: "Quick one, is the app down?" He answered and returned to the code. The chain of clues had slipped. Twenty minutes later: "Sorry, one more, can I tell customers it's fixed?" He answered. Again, he lost his place. At noon he walked to her desk. "I want to help, but each ping costs me about twenty minutes to get back in. Can we do a check-in at eleven and three?" Amara looked surprised, then nodded. "I had no idea."

qa.q: What was Santiago debugging?
qa.a: He was debugging a payment error.

qa.q: What was Santiago feeling after the second message?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and scattered, having lost the chain of clues again.

qa.q: What would you advise others who work with someone doing deep work?
qa.a: Save questions for agreed check-in times, like Santiago's eleven and three, unless something is truly urgent.

qa.q: How does Amara see her quick questions?
qa.a: Amara thought they were small and harmless, and is surprised to learn each one cost Santiago about twenty minutes.

grounding: Shows a worker losing focus each time a colleague sends a quick question and asking for fixed check-in times.

passage:
In the school office, Lakshmi was building next term's timetable, the hardest job of the year. Forty teachers, twenty-two classes, three labs, and a science teacher who could only come after ten. At 11:15 she was finally seeing how the lab slots could fit.
Ping. "Lakshmi, quick question, what's the Wi-Fi password?" It was Usha, from accounts. Lakshmi answered. When she looked back at the grid, the pattern had gone. It took twenty minutes to find it again.
At 12:05, ping: "Which form is for leave?" Then at 12:40: "Is the principal in?"
Each question took one minute to answer. Each time, Lakshmi lost the thread of the timetable for much longer. By lunch she had fixed only two classes.
After lunch she walked over to Usha's desk. "Can we try something? Keep a list of your questions and bring them to me at three. I'm stuck in the timetable till then."
Usha looked surprised. "I thought they were tiny."
"They are. Getting back isn't."

qa.q: How many teachers did the timetable have to cover?
qa.a: Forty teachers.

qa.q: How did Lakshmi feel each time the pattern disappeared?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt frustrated, losing the thread and needing twenty minutes to find it again after a one-minute question.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi suggest, and why is it a good fix?
qa.a: Lakshmi asked Usha to keep a list and bring questions at three, so the deep work isn't broken again and again.

qa.q: How did Usha see the questions before this conversation?
qa.a: Usha thought they were tiny, not realising how much time Lakshmi lost getting back into the timetable.

grounding: Shows a worker deep in a hard task who is pinged repeatedly with quick questions and loses much more time regaining focus each time.
